title_original: Skydance Will Need International Films to Supply Theatrical Release Pledge, Raine’s Joe Ravitch Predicts: ‘Those Are Big Investments’

blocks.text: One of the key promises David Ellison made to the industry in the lead-up to his heavily scrutinized merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers was that the newly-formed Skydance would release at least 30 films theatrically per year . To ensure that he delivers on the promise, the studio magnate will need to look beyond Hollywood, said top entertainment business investor Joe Ravitch .

blocks.text: Ravitch, who is the co-founder and partner of the Raine Group , a global merchant bank focused exclusively on technology, media and telecommunications, gave an insightful keynote talk on the first day of the Doha Film Festival ’s Industry Days.

blocks.text: “Paramount-Warner is committing to 30 theatrical releases a year,” he said. “I would guarantee you they are going to need international films to succeed as part of the world plan for national releases. And those are big investments by them. They are going to be looking to the world and partners to help feed that pipeline across multiple genres.”

Ravitch cited this gap as one of the key opportunities contributing to a golden window for Arab cinema to fulfill its international potential. Another, even more pressing one, is the streamers’ growing interest in the Global South after having exhausted their subscriber base in the Western world, particularly Netflix . Last month, the major platform’s shares hit a two-year low , with the concerning numbers coming a few days after a massive round of layoffs that saw the American powerhouse dismiss key executives such as chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin.

links.text: Last month, the major platform’s shares hit a two-year low

blocks.text: “The next wave for the streamers is the Global South,” said Ravitch. “Netflix stock is down. Why? Because they’ve basically matured and have hit [all] subscription levels they’re ever going to hit in Western Europe and the United States. They are focused on Asia; they are focused on Africa, the Middle East. The same is true for all the streamers. That’s where they see subscriber growth happening, so that’s where they need to get into that kind of content.”

This movement is even more interesting to Arab execs given that streamers are flocking to the region at a time when the “Hollywood monoculture is over,” he noted, adding how films like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “The Odyssey” will always top global box office charts, but “the next 10 films in a particular market are going to be local, and the streamers know that,” said the veteran. “If all the streamers show up in a market and deliver Hollywood content, they are not going to succeed.”

The world of tentpoles, Ravitch noted, is also eroding. Getting “big stars” to do “superhero movies” based on IP is no longer the easiest route to success in Hollywood. “We’ve seen this through ‘Backrooms,’ ‘Obsession,’ and other small-budget, YouTube movies succeeding beyond anybody’s wildest imagination. That’s a trend that will continue.”

The end of an era of over-reliance on stars is pivotal to the Middle East’s strategy to internationalize its industry, given that many countries in the region have opted to kickstart their markets by attracting big-gun Hollywood names either to shoot in their territory or promote it as a destination. “I think there have been a lot of missteps, to be honest,” said Ravitch of the strategy, refusing to cite any countries as an example of such practice. “It’s not about getting Tom Cruise to shoot a movie,” he observed.

“There’s been too much of a race to the bottom historically of ‘let’s get a famous movie star to come shoot this movie here’ as opposed to a sort of bottom-up approach,” he continued. This strategy is inefficient because the Hollywood films shot in Arab countries tend to be generic, characterless representations of the region that lead audiences to believe they might have been shot elsewhere.
Audiences can just as easily believe films have been shot in other popular production hubs such as Hungary, Italy and China, added the exec.

“[Productions] will go wherever it’s cheapest to shoot the film,” he said. “It doesn’t develop any kind of organic organization or systematized way where people are going to [focus] on the local culture.”

Focusing on developing local creativity, while also feeding from the know-how of international execs is the strongest way forward, especially in a market that has a key advantage: demand driven by a native audience coupled with demand from streamers. “What’s exciting to me about Arab culture, having done this in China, Korea, India and other places, is that you actually have a market here,” Ravitch pointed out.

“Whether it’s the Arab diaspora or Arab-speaking markets, there’s real disposable income and a common culture,” he said. The Arab world is a huge market, with around 500 million Arabic speakers worldwide, including a significant diasporic population in the U.S. and Europe, who also want to see themselves and their culture represented on screen.

There is, however, one key issue: streamers have famously entered international markets without sharing creative rights or long-term revenue with local makers. Industries in massive markets like Brazil, Netflix’s second-largest subscriber base, have been trying to regulate streamers for years without success.

Sitting in the audience, chairman and chief executive officer of AGC Studio Stuart Ford asked Ravitch about this “wrinkle in the system,” which he described as: “Streaming doesn’t share in the revenues. So ultimately you have local sectors and local stakeholders such as the Film Committee [in Qatar] [who] will invest in local content, develop it, finance it, but ultimately, if they want the global audience as the industry stands today, they’re gonna give up most of the upside.”

Stuart brought up the case of “Squid Game.” The massively popular series skyrocketed Korean production company Firstman Studio to global prominence, but Netflix owns the rights to the franchise. “They gave away the goose that laid the golden egg,” said Ravitch.

“One of my good friends at Property Media has a top show on Apple, one of the top shows on Paramount, and he makes no money because he got 120% cost,” he added. “So he’ll never make any. That’s a systemic problem we have.”

“As we start at the infancy of really building the more mature market for Arab storytelling and Arab culture, it’s something to be thoughtful about and careful about in how to avoid that and how to create an environment where all the streamers sort of want to be in this market.”
